newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's SEC sets up enforcement department.
newsitem.headline: Russia's SEC sets up enforcement department.

text.p: The head of Russia's main securities watchdog said on Tuesday he had set up a special enforcement department to help tighten up the vast country's often chaotic securities market.

Dmitry Vasilyev, chairman of the Federal Commission for the Securities Market, also said a draft regulation on introducing a unified depositary system would be ready by September 1 and the number of stock exchanges was likely to fall in the next year.

"The main priority is law enforcement," Vasilyev told Reuters. "That's why we set up an enforcement department. We try to tackle big scandals. It (the department) is not very big so far but it will have about 30 people."
Russia is keen to bring more order to the securities markets to provide transparency and reduce risk for domestic and foreign investors.

Vasilyev said the commission's role in enforcement was difficult because many Russians did not understand the concepts of insider trading and conflict of interest. Neither was properly legislated for so far and regulation would be hard. He did not give examples of cases the department had handled.
"I think insider trading is a really difficult problem," he said. "I think it will be settled after the next big scandal. The market develops from scandal to scandal."

On unifying the depositary system, Vasilyev said: "I think we have more or less favourable conditions to introduce this concept. But it depends which concept wins... I think the decision will be reached this summer."

He said his commission, the Central Bank, Finance Ministry and market professionals were studying various models. A draft regulation would be ready by September 1, a deadline set by First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, who is also finance minister.
Asked about the proliferation of securities exchanges, he said: "There is no doubt that in the next year the number of exchanges will be reduced drastically."
Of 30 operating in Moscow now about three would remain. There would be one each in the major cities across Russia, making about 15 in all.

Apart from the over-the-counter electronic Russian Trading System, which is Russia's main equities market, the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX) has started trading shares. MICEX is already the main market for government securities, as well as an important floor for currency trading.
Several other exchanges in Moscow and St Petersburg trade futures and options on currencies, T-bills and equities, but many other exchanges are effectively moribund.
Vasilyev, who has ministerial rank, also said the commission had set up 15 regional branches to deal with prospectuses and collect company reports.

His headquarters was working on setting up a technical centre to hold the information electronically for investors and other interested parties, such as news agencies. There would be no commercial fee. --Martin Nesirky, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
